newsitem.title: USA: Starr staffers regret asking about Jones - report.
newsitem.headline: Starr staffers regret asking about Jones - report.

text.p: Aides to Whitewater special prosecutor Kenneth Starr admit it was "unwise" of FBI agents to ask about Paula Jones while probing then Arkansas Gov. Bill Clinton's private life for Starr, Newsweek said Sunday.

Between last November and February, Starr had the FBI interview every Arkansas state trooper who had served on the governor's detail in the mid- to late 1980s, asking about Clinton's unpublicised contacts with people, including six women with whom he allegedly had affairs. The Washington Post revealed the prosecutor's "new line of inquiry" on its front page last week.

Newsweek, which is published by the Washington Post Co., concluded in its forthcoming issue that "in some respects the Post story was overstated." The FBI agents asked more questions about men than women, it said, and passed little of what one trooper alleged about Clinton's private life on to their superiors.

But the magazine said aides to Starr conceded it had been "unwise" of the investigators to ask about Paula Jones, the former Arkansas state employee who is suing Clinton for alleged sexual harassment.
Both Newsweek and Time, in its new issue, said that within two weeks Starr was likely to release his final report on the death in 1993 of White House lawyer Vince Foster.
The report, delayed because of doubts about the reliability of FBI crime laboratories, will find that Foster committed suicide, according to Newsweek.

As for Jones, a New Yorker writer has found a former office colleague of hers who recalls her as being elated, not upset, soon after her alleged encounter with Clinton at a Little Rock hotel, the magazine said.

The pace of Starr's investigation came under attack on NBC-TV's "Today" show Sunday from Democratic Sens. Richard Durbin of Illinois and Bob Kerrey of Nebraska, who also said the iterviewing of state troopers was "completely inappropriate and unacceptable."
Sen. Don Nickles, a Republican from Oklahoma, agreed the probe needed to end soon but said the Clinton administration had contributed to the slow going.
"He (Starr) needs to wrap the investigation up or bring it to a close," Nickles said.
